what_its_for: Ponatinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of blood cancer called chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) or a type of leukemia called Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL). It works by blocking certain signals in cancer cells that tell them to grow and multiply, helping to slow or stop the cancer.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablet whole with or without food. Do not crush, break, or chew the tablet. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember. If you vomit after taking your dose, do not take another dose — just take your next scheduled dose at the regular time.
dosing: Your doctor will prescribe the right dose for you based on your specific type of leukemia, your response to treatment, and any side effects you may have. The usual starting dose is 45 mg once daily, but your doctor may lower your dose to 30 mg or 15 mg over time to reduce side effects. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store ponatinib at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Store tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges (often found in marmalades) while taking this medicine, as they can increase the amount of ponatinib in your blood and worsen side effects. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medicines you take, including vitamins and herbal supplements, because many drugs can interact with ponatinib. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine — use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after your last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking ponatinib. Avoid activities that could increase your risk of bleeding or injury.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: chest pain, shortness of breath, or pain in your arm or jaw (possible heart attack or blood clot signs); sudden numbness, weakness, or trouble speaking (possible stroke signs); severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting (possible pancreas problems); vision changes or eye pain; yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe tiredness (possible liver problems); unusual bleeding or bruising; high blood pressure readings; slow healing of wounds; signs of infection such as fever or chills. This is not a complete list — call your doctor anytime you feel something is not right.
when_it_works: You will have regular blood tests and checkups so your doctor can see how well the medicine is working. Some people start to see improvements in their lab results within a few weeks, but it may take several months to see the full benefit. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel well — stopping too early can allow the cancer to return.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Ponatinib can harm an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Women who can become pregnant must use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Liver problems: If you have liver disease, your doctor may adjust your dose or monitor you more closely, as ponatinib is processed by the liver. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as blood clots, heart problems, and bleeding, so extra monitoring may be needed. Children: The safety and effectiveness of ponatinib in children have not been fully established — ask your doctor for guidance.
